Vision & Strategy
This tab answers: what game are we making, for whom, and what will we refuse to build?

Fill 1.1 last. Start with 1.3, because pillars decide what belongs in 1.4 and 1.7. Leave 1.6 and 1.9 in draft until the prototype is playable; market numbers and KPI targets change faster than the design.
1.1 One-page pitch
Keep every answer to one clause. Read the finished table aloud in three minutes; anything you stumble on is a decision the team has not made.

{{Curious players aged 9 and up who like tidy, low-pressure puzzles.}}

{{A base-builder you can finish in a weekend}}; {{premium, one price}}.

blocks.x: Why it matters: this is the only page every discipline reads before kickoff, so a disagreement here costs an hour instead of a milestone. Good pitch test: a producer can repeat the logline from memory, an artist can name the mood, and an engineer can name the risk. If the table needs a second page, it is a plan, not a pitch.
{{A stranded repair robot has one shift to make a broken moon base breathe again.}} *One character, one deadline, one verb, one stake: that is why it works.*

Run the read as a meeting, not a recital. Give each discipline one question: design asks whether the loop is clear, art asks whether the mood is achievable, engineering asks what could break, and production asks what must be cut. Write the answers in the margin; the pitch is done when the margin is empty.
1.2 High concept

Write the elevator pitch before the feature list. Keep it under 100 words, name one protagonist and one problem, and stop before the twist. The X meets Y line is a shortcut for tone, not a promise of features.

Elevator pitch (max 100 words): {{A small repair robot wakes on a silent lunar outpost with one working air tank and a crew arriving at sunrise. Salvage cargo, reconnect pipes, and coax each room back to life across six shifts. Every choice spends something: power, air, or time. The base is small, the problems are legible, and the ending is a place you rebuilt with your own hands.}}
X meets Y: {{the tidy spatial puzzles of Unpacking}} meets {{the resource pressure of a one-room survival game}}, wrapped in {{a toy-like lunar diorama}}.
Why it matters: the pitch is the tie-breaker when two features compete for the same week. If a feature cannot be explained through the pitch, it belongs in a prototype, not the schedule.
The player promise

x: You will always understand why a room failed.
Every repair makes the base visibly warmer and busier.
A missed shift costs a retry, never a save file.

blocks.x: Minute to minute

x: Scan the room: read the air gauge, the blocked vents, and the one glowing fault.
Choose: spend a battery, reroute a pipe, or dismantle a crate for parts.
Place: drag the part onto the grid; the preview shows the new air path before you commit.
Confirm and watch: the fan spins up, the gauge climbs, the shift timer keeps running.

blocks.x: Good high concept: a stranger can describe the game to a friend after one hearing, and the description contains a verb. If the description is only a setting, rewrite it until someone is doing something.
1.3 Design pillars

Write three to five pillars, no more. Each pillar must be able to reject a feature the team likes. If two pillars can never conflict, merge them. Test each against the last three arguments the team had.

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.x: A pillar that cannot reject a feature is a value, not a pillar. If every idea passes the test, rewrite the pillar until something fails.

blocks.x: Decision test

Put every proposed feature through three questions, in order: Does it make one pillar stronger? Which pillar does it weaken? What do we remove to pay for it? A feature that strengthens none goes to the cut list, not the backlog.
Kill rule: {{if a feature fails two pillars, we cut it this milestone, even if it is already prototyped.}}
What good looks like: each pillar has a scar. Name one feature the team killed because of it, and one argument it settled. A pillar with no scar is a poster, not a constraint.
1.4 Non-goals and scope boundaries

Write non-goals as sentences a new hire can act on. Name the genre you are not making, the feature you will not build, and the audience you will not chase. Revisit this list at every milestone; it is cheaper to defend than to rediscover.
Non-goals protect the pillars. They are not insults to good ideas; they are a promise that the team will not spend this budget on them.

x: This is not an open-world builder. The outpost is one map with fixed rooms.
This is not a survival game. Air is a puzzle resource, not a hunger bar.
This is not a narrative RPG. Characters speak in short radio lines, not dialogue trees.
This is not a live-service game. There is no season pass, store, or daily login.
This is not a horror game. Alarms and darkness signal problems, never threat.

blocks.x: Cut-list philosophy

Keep a ranked cut list from day one. Cut from the bottom, never from the pillars. A feature is safe only when it has an owner, a test, and a place in the build; everything else is optional by default. When the schedule slips, cut the bottom item without a meeting.

Write each non-goal as a refusal with a reason: we will not add online co-op because it doubles the test matrix and the puzzle needs one decision-maker. A refusal without a reason invites the same request next month.
Scope guardrails

blocks.x: What good looks like: a contractor can read this section and know which request to decline without asking you. If every non-goal needs a meeting to interpret, rewrite it as a sentence with a verb.
1.5 Target audience and motivations

Describe two segments, not a demographic. For each, name what they want to feel and what they will tolerate. Then check the age rating: the youngest player you name sets the reading level, text size, and failure tone.
Primary: {{players who play puzzle games to unwind and finish something in a sitting}}. Secondary: {{parents and educators looking for a calm co-play game with a child}}.

blocks.x: Accessibility needs

x: Remappable controls, one-hand mode, and no held input longer than {{1 s}}.
Subtitles for radio lines, with speaker labels and a size slider.
Colour-blind safe status icons: shape plus colour, never colour alone.
Assist mode that slows timers by {{50%}} without changing rewards.
Minimum body text {{18 px at 1080p}}, scalable to {{200%}}.

blocks.x: Age rating: {{PEGI 3 / ESRB E}} if there is no violence, no fear, and no online chat. Any threat imagery or jump scare pushes the rating up and narrows the audience; decide before art production, not after.
What good looks like: every accessibility feature has a platform setting, a default, and a test. A promise in this section without a menu entry is marketing.

Pick five comps the team has actually played. For each, write what you borrow and what you avoid. Prices are launch prices in your largest market; date them, because they age badly.

blocks.x: Date every price and note the region. A comp table without dates becomes a fiction within two store sales, and the team starts pricing against ghosts.

Choose comps that share two of three traits: audience, session length, or price. A comp that shares only a mood teaches you nothing about the market. Play each for at least an hour and note the moment you stopped.
Differentiation: {{we are the only cozy base game where the air network is the puzzle, not the backdrop; one screen, one shift, one visible consequence.}}

Positioning map: draw two axes, {{pressure (calm to urgent)}} and {{scale (one room to open world)}}. Plot the five comps, then mark the empty quadrant you want. If two comps already sit there, sharpen an axis until the space is real.
What good looks like: the comps table changes one decision. If it only confirms what the team already believed, add a comp that scares you and write the avoid column first.

1.9 Success metrics and risks
Choose three to five metrics you can measure in the demo. A target without a measurement method is a wish. For risks, write the mitigation as an action with a date, not a sentiment.

Targets are for the demo, not the launch. A demo that hits its completion target tells you the first hour works; it says nothing about the ending. Keep one metric per audience promise, and delete any metric nobody would act on.

Separate leading from lagging metrics. Wishlist conversion is lagging; time to first repair is leading. Put one leading metric per pillar on the dashboard, and review it weekly. A dashboard with twelve numbers is a screensaver, not a decision tool.
